video_title: ⚡️ The 2026 Software Factory Infra Stack — Zach Lloyd, Warp.dev
gist: Warp CEO Zach Lloyd lays out 'software factories' — declarative, cloud-run agentic coding systems defined in code — and a six-layer infra stack (factory-as-code, agent trace store, MCP/data access, pluggable sandbox compute, open inference/harness, improvement/scoring, orchestrator, access points). He shares Warp's internal metrics (cost per PR cut from ~$80 to ~$15-20, PR throughput +40% in a month with flat revert rate, 60% of work started in Slack) and argues pure coding-agent businesses are uneconomic versus subsidized lab subscriptions.

insights.claim: Zach Lloyd defines a software factory as a cloud agentic system in which agent roles across the software lifecycle are defined with some autonomy, and which is measurable and closed-loop so teams can tune and benchmark it over time.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Shifts AI coding from individual tool use to team-level infrastructure.

insights.claim: Most companies are trying to build some internal software factory, but most engineers still use Claude Code, Codex or similar individually in local setups without centralization.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Large greenfield market for centralized agent orchestration and observability.
insights.quote: most of the world is trying to build some sort of internal software factory or set of software factories.

insights.claim: Warp's model is one factory per product surface, each with its repos, skills, MCPs and a workflow (triage, specking, implementation) defined in a YAML file, with work entering via Slack, Linear, Jira, GitHub, API or MCP.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Factory-as-code is positioned like Terraform for agentic development.

insights.claim: Lloyd sees the software factory as a new layer in the developer infrastructure stack sitting one level back from CI/CD, which he expects most companies to adopt.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Signals a new developer-infra category analogous to CI/CD.
insights.quote: It kind of sits one level back from like where CI/CD is, but I think most companies will have something like this for software development.

insights.claim: Lloyd predicts engineering will split into product engineering and 'factory engineering', where engineers build the system that builds the software rather than the software directly.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Platform/DevX teams become the key buyers and a new engineering discipline emerges.

insights.claim: Lloyd's recommended stack: declarative factory-as-code at the bottom, then a store of agent conversations and artifacts, MCP data access with org-level permissions, pluggable sandbox compute, open inference and harness choice, an improvement layer, an orchestrator, and multiple access points.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Provides a reference architecture defining where vendors can compete.

insights.claim: Defining the factory in code yields versioning, branching and revert, plus the ability for coding agents to propose pull requests against the factory definition itself, the foundation of a self-improving factory.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Self-improving agent systems require declarative definitions.
insights.quote: because it's in code, coding agents can suggest improvements to it.

insights.claim: Warp uses Namespace as its primary agent sandbox but recommends making compute pluggable for providers such as Daytona, Modal or E2B, and supporting Mac VMs for iOS computer-use testing.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Sandbox providers are becoming commoditized, swappable components.

insights.claim: Many companies have pre-existing commits with Anthropic, OpenAI or Google they want to burn down, so Warp lets customers bring their own inference provider or harness, including any ACP-compatible harness.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Enterprise inference commitments drive demand for model-agnostic orchestration layers.

insights.claim: Lloyd says the orchestrator is only one piece of the platform, though people sometimes talk about it as if it were the whole thing.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Orchestration alone is not a defensible product; measurement and improvement layers matter.
insights.quote: Sometimes people talk about the orchestrator like it's the whole platform. I think it's a piece of it.

insights.claim: Centralizing agent traces enables metrics such as DORA metrics, human touches per merged PR, throughput, and cost per PR sliced by person, automation and SDLC stage.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Cost per PR becomes the key unit-economics KPI for AI coding.

insights.claim: Warp's 'scorers' are LLM-as-judge online evals that retroactively grade sampled historical agent runs for failure modes like redundant tests, verbosity or code quality, with sampling rates to control cost.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Online evals on real runs replace vibes-based tool selection.

insights.claim: Coding agents commonly write redundant tests while figuring out an implementation and leave them in, bloating codebases and wasting tokens.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Known agent failure mode that adds hidden cost and maintenance burden.

insights.claim: Warp's self-improvement agents found 54 failure cases where its triage step would have been better if the triager could spawn a sub-agent, and proposed a pull request to the factory definition.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Demonstrates closed-loop agentic self-optimization in practice.

insights.claim: Benchmarking real company runs across model and harness combinations showed a GPT-5-series model at 95% correctness for about $6 per task versus a GLM model at 93% for about $2, which can feed a model or harness routing strategy.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Cheaper open models can be near-parity on company workloads, favoring routing strategies.

insights.claim: Lloyd argues the industry must move from vibes-based debates over models and harnesses to measurement on a company's own workloads.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Demand will grow for internal benchmarking and eval tooling.

insights.claim: When Warp first adopted factories it cost about $80 per PR due to overusing Opus (including for triage) and too many sub-agents; tuning brought it to roughly $15-20 per PR.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Model choice and agent topology can cut AI coding cost ~75%.
insights.quote: it was costing us about $80 per PR because we were using like Opus where we shouldn't have.

insights.claim: Warp's PR throughput rose 40% over the last month while its revert rate did not increase.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Evidence that measured tuning can raise output without hurting quality.

insights.claim: About 60% of Warp's work now starts in Slack, reflecting a strategy of bringing the factory into existing knowledge-work tools as headless, API- and MCP-driven infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Collaboration tools become the front door for agentic engineering.
insights.quote: we're doing like 60% of our work is starting in Slack.

insights.claim: Lloyd puts the floor for software-factory infrastructure at roughly 5-10 engineers; growth-stage startups of 10-100 engineers on Slack/Linear/Jira can self-serve, while very large companies require implementation work.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Defines the ICP for factory platforms: scaling mid-size engineering orgs.

insights.claim: Companies with very bespoke infrastructure and large internal developer teams, such as Uber or Ramp, are poor fits because they build their own.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Largest tech firms are build-not-buy for this category.

insights.claim: The host says paying by API is 5-50x more expensive than using subscriptions, with a $200 plan yielding about $8,000 of API-equivalent usage, and small teams rotate many $200 subs.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Lab subsidies on subscriptions distort coding-agent economics.
insights.quote: Like you get for like a $200 plan you get 8,000 of API.

insights.claim: Lloyd does not want to be in the pure coding-agent business because independents cannot compete with labs' subsidized pricing; he says Cursor realized this and became a model lab, and the host says only Cognition and OpenCode remain independent.
insights.speaker: Zach Lloyd
insights.so_what: Independent coding-agent vendors face existential margin pressure; value shifts to optimization/infra layers.
